General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
  • Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s?
  • "Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today.".

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?".

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

Industry observers note that the facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

Sources indicate that there are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

Recent findings suggest that however, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

In a recent development, over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

In a recent development, despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

According to recent reports, he suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he mentioned. "Even if it means making sacrifices.".

This article was originally published in German.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

It has been revealed that on his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

In a recent development, city’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Recent findings suggest that guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Maresca noted: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”.

Industry observers note that when asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca stated: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”.

In a recent development, while much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

Industry observers note that it was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

It has been revealed that emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”.

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

Industry observers note that the home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

However, football managers persist with the idea that there is another ineffable reason that decides who deserves what. Enzo Maresca is apparently no different.

“I was not here in the past but today I think we deserved something more.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that however, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Sources indicate that emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea have joined Manchester United in monitoring Scott McTominay as uncertainty grows over the midfielder’s long-term future at Napoli.

The Scotland international has transformed his reputation since leaving Old Trafford in 2024, becoming one of Serie A’s most influential midfielders and helping Napoli win the Scudetto in his first full season.

However, contract talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, opening the door to a possible Premier League return in 2027.

According to TEAMtalk, McTominay has around 18 months remaining on his Napoli contract and negotiations over an extension remain some distance from an agreement.

Intermediaries are already exploring possible destinations, with Chelsea and Manchester United among the clubs informed about his potential availability.

Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning.
  • But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage.
  • Industry observers note that for 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer states she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

Industry observers note that for 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

It has been revealed that opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

Sources indicate that in 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

It has been revealed that espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, noted the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

According to recent reports, on the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law.".

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security problem.".

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas noted.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

Recent findings suggest that this suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

Sources indicate that but Tas noted that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment.".

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mauricio Pochettino will officially join Manchester United after the current United States men's national team camp concludes, bringing an end to his two-year tenure in the job that was headlined by this year's World Cup on home soil.His final games in charge will be the two-legged Concacaf Nations League semifinals against Haiti, the first of which will take place on Saturday at Miami's Nu Stadium while the second will be on Tuesday at Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.

In a recent development, for the USMNT, the timing is awkward. Though the next World Cup is still four years away, Pochettino signed a new four-year deal in August and is currently with the team at U.S. Soccer's national training center in the suburbs of Atlanta. He spent the week with the USMNT while his representatives worked out a deal for him to join United.

In a recent development, "That news kind of got sprung on us, like the rest of the world, I'd say," Robinson said. "Similar things happened in the past, happened at the World Cup where huge teams lose their manager and they start looking at possible candidates and for us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means we're very lucky to work with a top-level manager but it never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it's the World Cup or whether it's going to be this camp.".

Pochettino was the first USMNT head coach with genuine international appeal, U.S. Soccer more often than not picking from a domestic talent pool in the team's modern history. His tenure has reflected just that – he became the federation's highest-paid coach ever when he initially joined in 2024, the salary and the scope of his role only increasing in his recent contract extension. U.S. Soccer surprisingly plucked him out of the European club game, where he had spent the entirety of his coaching career beforehand, making a name for himself at Tottenham Hotspur before later stops at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. Naturally, clubs of that ilk never lost interest and over the course of his time with the USMNT, he was linked to a handful of jobs. The most notable approach came from AC Milan, who were considering the move in the build-up to the World Cup but ultimately hired ex-Manchester United coach Ruben Amorim instead.

Industry observers note that "Even when we first met a couple summers ago, there were lots of other people interested in having Mauricio and team join," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson said in May. "He had standing offers from other places to come. He wanted to be here. He's a massive believer in what we're doing at U.S. Soccer. He's a big believer in soccer in America and he's a big believer in this men's team and so, throughout this entire process, when you have top-class talent, whether it's salespeople, whether it's marketing people or whether it's coaches, other organizations want them and throughout this, Mauricio and team have been incredibly transparent. They've been great partners and are, of course, excited about the summer … There's been a longer list of outreach than what has even been reported and so they've been great about that.".

Pochettino has also been open about his desire to return to the Premier League during his stint with the USMNT, something the move to United will accomplish.

United are right now in the relegation zone with one win in 10 games, the least of any team in the Premier League this season.

In a recent development, pochettino's track record with the USMNT is not exactly notable – he has 21 wins in 45 games, nearly all of them against teams below them in the FIFA rankings. They stumbled in a variety of ways when they attempted to punch above their weight, most notably in the World Cup round of 16 loss to Belgium that was tinged by the Folarin Balogun affair. His attempts to lead the USMNT to a statement-making run at a World Cup on home soil were mixed at best, since the team could not pass the last 16 hurdle they have been stuck at since 2010, but Pochettino still found a way to recalibrate the U.S. team in his two years in charge.

It has been revealed that the specifics of the round of 16 elimination were a surprise, even if the exit was not. The U.S. team's player pool, talented as it was at the World Cup, was not considered amongst the world's elites so a genuinely deep run over the summer felt improbable. Pochettino, though, managed to get the best out of the group and had the USMNT playing in a way it rarely had previously – in an entertaining, high-intensity, attack-minded system. The style is a hallmark of Pochettino's coaching career but has been historically difficult to integrate at the international level, with teams usually gathering for 10 days at a time, weeks or months apart, and has historically not been the USMNT's strategy. Pochettino's predecessor Gregg Berhalter, for example, was more reserved in his tactical approach and before him, the U.S. team were known more for grit than style.

Slowly but surely, Pochettino's approach worked with the generation of players Berhalter brought in. He correctly identified that the player pool's strengths were in attack, forwards Balogun and Christian Pulisic continuing to serve as central figures for the team. More notably, though, Pochettino found use for players Berhalter had previously cast aside – midfielder Malik Tillman became a key player, his versatility something Pochettino counted as an asset. Forward Ricardo Pepi also rose up the ranks in the build-up to the World Cup, his first after being one of the last omissions from Berhalter's 2022 team.

Industry observers note that pochettino's legacy might actually be the player pool shakeup he oversaw on the road to the World Cup, which felt rushed because of the short timeline but was ultimately useful. Defender Alex Freeman was the breakout of the Pochettino years, going from relative obscurity at Orlando City to a World Cup starter and goalscorer in less than 500 days. Midfielder Sebastian Berhalter, the son of Pochettino's predecessor, was not on the national team's radar until his first call-up in 2025 and looks like a national team fixture for years to come. The player pool expansion project will only get more exciting from here with the USMNT's up-and-comers, with some like Cavan Sullivan and Adri Mehmeti poised to be some of the best players in the history of the men's program.

Sources indicate that the coach's departure will sting in some ways, but his tenure ensured that the USMNT would be in a position of strength, which was hardly the case when he arrived. He inherited a team that had lost its way after a group stage exit in the Copa America and will leave behind a team with a clear enough roadmap to the 2030 World Cup. The Pochettino years prove that the next head coach should primarily be a strong tactical fit, no matter the candidate's global appeal, because he was right to identify that an attack-minded approach would suit the player pool. That's especially true with the up-and-comers since many of the brightest prospects are attackers.

In a recent development, there is no reason U.S. Soccer should not hire the best fit for the job but for perhaps the first time in the program's history, the USMNT's prospects might truly rest with the players at their disposal. Pochettino's successor will be chiefly tasked with getting the best out of them, much as he did with the U.S. team's core. As an exciting generation of talent finds their footing with the senior team, that's exactly how it should be.

Industry News: Can Mauricio Pochettino replicate hallmark intensity he brought to USMNT with Manchester United?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, from the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system.
  • According to recent reports, too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better.
  • Manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, from the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system. Indeed, there is such potential for misdiagnosis when assessing running statistics that senior figures at more than one of the best recruiting clubs in England consider their worth to be, at best, dubious.

According to recent reports, too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better. You know who didn't have to peg it all that often? Sergio Busquets, perhaps the best defensive midfielder of his generation, plying his trade for the majority of his career at Barcelona. Keep the ball, read the game, control the territory and you will very rapidly find the other team covering plenty more kilometers than you.

Manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season. If there were any correlation between distance covered and results, then the relegation race would be even more exciting than it is shaping up to be, given that Liverpool sit below United on that measure and Manchester City above them. It is quite hard to believe that United are winning fewer games compared to last year (when they had nearly 10% less possession it should be noted) because each player is covering about 45 meters fewer per game. Physical data might not be linked to team quality, then, but it might tell us something relevant if, for instance, United were to hire a coach who prizes dynamic players and demands an intense press at the very top of the pitch. A Mauricio Pochettino type, if you will. The soon-to-be former United States men's national team head coach, handed the task of extricating Manchester United from the relegation zone before molding a contender, is defined by the aggression and energy of his charges. It is why he was the perfect match for a young Tottenham side with a point to prove. It is why Paris Saint-Germain and the Neymar-Kylian Mbappe axis was such an obviously awkward fit from the off.

Industry observers note that it is also a template that has worked even when there was cause for skepticism. You couldn't have players sprinting their way across SoFi after the rigors of a club season, stated those who doubted the USMNT. He didn't ask much of his team, just "to use your brain while physically, you were killing yourself," as Tim Ream, then 38, said in the summer.

Tell you what, though, it worked. The United States' World Cup campaign might have ended at about the time and in the fashion that most expected, but at their best, they were pressing dynamos. Their 10.16 passes allowed per defensive action (PPDA) -- a measure of press intensity -- placed them sixth among the 48 teams at the World Cup, rubbing shoulders with the likes of Germany, Spain and Uruguay, coached by Pochettino's mentor and high priest of the high press Marcelo Bielsa. No team that reached the knockouts forced their opponents to misplace a higher proportion of their passes than the U.S., 22.8%.

Pochettino might have framed much of his work around changing the culture of the USMNT, but that was a job that was easier to do with a player pool that suited his needs. His squad was strong, organized and, most importantly of all, athletic.

According to recent reports, that is not a term that is particularly associated with Manchester United. Indeed, according to Gradient Sports, one of the leading external providers of physical data in football, Pochettino's new team is the least athletic in the Premier League. Based on Gradient's athleticism score -- which combines a host of physical data points including accelerations and decelerations, sprint distance and max speed -- United and Nottingham Forest are cut adrift from the rest of the league. In average max speed of outfield players, United also rank 19th out of 20, 5% slower than the fleet-footed Bournemouth and Liverpool.

According to recent reports, the months to come may prove that United look unathletic because that's how Michael Carrick wanted them to play, controlling possession and building more steadily than the sides who rushed headfirst into any counter that came their way. Instinctively, though, that does not feel like the United of Harry Maguire, Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo, does it?

According to recent reports, the three center backs who have started the bulk of United's Premier League games this season -- Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven -- all rank around the bottom third or lower of players in their position in terms of top speed, accelerations and decelerations and percentage of runs at high speeds (20-25 km/h), according to Gradient data. It is a similar story for the midfielders, particularly Andrey Santos, Mainoo and Tielemans. The one central midfield option with an impressive athletic profile, Carlos Baleba, is out injured. It seemed bitterly ironic that Baleba's hamstring went after a driving run through midfield. The sheer act of high-intensity running does sometimes look like it puts an unbearable strain on United legs.

That might be why they do it so little. Opta judges that Santos applies pressure to 56.2% of his opponents' touches, Tielemans 56.8%, Bruno Fernandes 57% and Mainoo 57.3%. All of them sit in the bottom 12 in the league among midfielders with 300 or more minutes. Marcus Rashford, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Amad Diallo occupy spots one, three, five and six in terms of the top flight's least pressing-y forwards.

Industry observers note that now, of course, Pochettino can adapt. After all, he has just implemented a surprisingly effective high press in a side captained by Ream (sorry, Tim!). A lot of the Chelsea squad he took over in 2023-24 did not look to be at ease hunting the ball, but he still had them above league average in PPDA, opponent pass completion, ball recoveries and in particular duel success in the final third. A bit more oomph is not beyond these United players, as they indicated last season.

However, it is particularly curious to finally alight on Pochettino, whom they could have hired at least half a dozen times in the past, when the squad seems so ill-suited to his principles. We might not be able to tell from physical data whether this team was giving its all for Carrick -- and, by extension, whether there is another gear for the newly introduced manager to drive them to -- but what we can see is certainly enough to raise the question of why the powers that be at United think that this is a squad ready to play Pochettino-style.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Owen and Frank Lampard are two of the most recognisable names in English football history, racking up 935 Premier League appearances between them, and the pair have naturally had a number of incredibly talented teammates in their time at the very top of the game.

Owen famously won the Ballon d'Or in 2001, after enjoying a prolific season at Liverpool. The pacey striker netted 158 goals in 297 appearances for the Reds, before going on to enjoy stints at Real Madrid, Newcastle United and Manchester United. He finished his career with a Premier League title, an FA Cup and two League Cups to his name.

Meanwhile, Lampard's illustrious career saw him become the most prolific goalscoring midfielder in Premier League history. He hung up his boots having scored 177 goals in the English top flight, whilst he also has a number of team accolades to his name, including three League titles and a Champions League triumph.

In a recent development, while the pair played alongside an array of exceptional, world-class players, there are always teammates that fall by the wayside — not everyone makes it to the very top and stays there. Former Leeds United star Paul Shepherd is among those who played with both ex-England stars and very much falls into this category.

Twenty-seven years after making his first team debut for Leeds at the age of 18, Shepherd was sentenced to nine years in prison.

Born in West Yorkshire, Shepherd joined the Whites' academy at a young age. He steadily progressed through the various youth ranks before going on to make a solitary appearance for the senior side under George Graham.

After uninspiring loan spells at Ayr United and Tranmere Rovers, Leeds parted ways with the full-back, allowing him to leave for the former club in 1999. He'd go on to enjoy stints at Scunthorpe United, Luton Town and Scarborough, as well as spending time in the lower leagues with various semi-professional Yorkshire clubs.

16 years after hanging up his boots, Shepherd's post-retirement life came crashing down when he was arrested and subsequently found guilty of conspiracy to supply Class A drugs.

It has been revealed that A defensively astute full-back at youth level, there was some level of excitement over what Shepherd could develop into as he approached the first team. His performances in the Leeds academy were garnering attention, and a month after taking over at Elland Road, Graham chose to acknowledge the defender by calling him up to a matchday squad.

In October 1996, the Whites travelled to North London to take on Graham's former club Arsenal at Highbury. Leeds may have lost 3-0, but the game marked a memorable occasion for Shepherd, who made his senior debut. Completing the entire 90 minutes, the right-back was strangely deployed as a forward, alongside legendary number nine Ian Rush.

Many thought that this game might serve as a launchpad for Shepherd's career at Elland Road, but it proved to be anything but. Graham inexplicably opted to leave the youngster out of the squad for the rest of the 1996/97 season, despite the player being properly integrated into the senior set-up at this point.

“George came into the club, by then I was a professional, and he literally never said two words to me,” Shepherd told Planet Football in 2020.

According to recent reports, "As a young kid, you just think ‘he doesn’t like me’. It was really hard to deal with. He [Graham] gave me my debut at Arsenal, but he never spoke to me once during the time I was there, before, during or after that game. Literally nothing. As an 18-year-old kid, I had no idea how to handle it, to be honest. It was a real shock to the system.”.

While Graham evidently wasn't fond of Shepherd, this lack of senior minutes at club level didn't prevent the Leeds academy graduate from making waves in the England youth set-up. In the summer of 1997, Shepherd was named in the Three Lions' squad for the FIFA World Youth Championship, held in Malaysia.

It has been revealed that the England squad consisted of the likes of Jamie Carragher, Danny Murphy and, of course, Owen. A year or so before that, Shepherd had been mixing it with Lampard in England's under-18s squad.

Industry observers note that despite being on a level playing field with these future stars, the Leeds man didn't develop in the same way some of his peers did. After Graham froze him out, Shepherd attempted to reignite his career in West Yorkshire by twice going on loan. Neither proved successful, and he eventually left his boyhood club to sign for Scottish outfit Ayr United.

Industry observers note that his exit from Leeds sparked the beginning of a six-year spell which saw Shepherd play for eight different clubs. After failing to make an appearance at Oldham, he spent time in non-league, at Scarborough, Leigh RMI, Harrogate Town and finally, Stalybridge Celtic.

Recent findings suggest that shepherd retired in 2005 after struggling to settle at a number of different clubs. In 2023, the ex-footballer was arrested for dealing large amounts of cocaine.

According to BBC News, Shepherd was found guilty of being a trusted courier for the drugs, involved in collecting and delivering cash for linchpin Carl O'Flaherty all over the UK.

The former Leeds star was jailed alongside three other men, with the criminal network uncovered after police stopped Shepherd and seized cocaine from his car. It was unearthed that O'Flaherty had led a wholesale drugs supply business for a number of years, and he was ultimately sentenced to 17 years and 10 months in prison.

Shepherd's sentence was less severe, although he was still jailed for nine years and six months after pleading guilty.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And that’s exactly how it panned out with just two minutes left on the clock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 18:01 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 18:10 EST, 21 November 2026.

FOR a team that just couldn’t find a way to get the ball into the net, no matter how they tried, it was always going to take a couple of jammy deflections or something out of the ordinary to get out of jail.

And that’s exactly how it panned out with just two minutes left on the clock. Rangers, tied at 1-1 and in danger of falling six points behind arch-rivals Celtic at the head of the Premiership, were throwing everything bar the kitchen sink at their hosts.

Balls were being blazed high and wide of the target. Chances were being passed up left, right and centre. It looked like Derek McInnes’ men were destined to rack up a third straight away draw in the league and take the club’s record to three years without a win at Fir Park when, in the 85th minute, substitute Findlay Curtis saw an effort parried by Alex Paulsen, Dujon Sterling blasted the rebound towards goal and Motherwell’s No 1 somehow flung an arm in the air and diverted it onto the crossbar.

It looked like the last throw of the dice. Until Ryan Naderi, who had suffered a miserable evening up to that point, made the difference.

A speculative shot from Badredine Bouanani from the edge of the area whacked off the outstretched boot of Martin Moormann and fell into the Czech internationalist’s path on the right.

His jabbed effort towards goal was nothing to write home about, but it carried just enough juice on it to whack off the hapless Moormann again, change direction and fly into the net.

Messy? Yes. Did Naderi care, though? Not a bit. He ran straight into the Rangers crowd behind the goal and lost himself in the relief and jubilation of a victory rescued from the fire.

That’s all that matters right now. Rangers won to keep up the pressure at the head of the table.

Naderi celebrates his late winner that snatched all three points for Rangers.

McInnes applauds the travelling supporters after his side kept pace with Celtic at the top.

However, there is a recurring problem with this squad. This game should have been out of sight, but missing chances and lacking that killer instinct manager McInnes demands remains a serious problem.

Just look at the stats. Rangers had 29 shots on goal in this affair and 11 on target. It should have been a procession, really. In the end, they only got through by the skin of their teeth.

There are times when these players look like they couldn’t hit a cow on the backside with a banjo and that is going to trip them up big-time in this title race unless they sort it out tout-suite.

They started like a runaway train in this game and got off to the perfect start with Manny Fernandez heading home from a corner within the first 10 minutes.

The problems started when Naderi, just nowhere as convincing in the role of main striker as he is when played with the likes of Kevin Kelsy, benched last night before a late cameo, up beside him, started missing sitters.

According to recent reports, jake Girdwood-Reich then levelled for Motherwell with pretty much their first forage upfield and it all got way more uncomfortable than it should have been. It is something McInnes is going to have to sort out.

The match started exactly the way McInnes would have wanted following the return from the international break with Rangers in the ascendancy from the first whistle and a goal to the good after eight minutes.

According to recent reports, it was also as straightforward and as simple a goal as you could wish to see. One from a set-piece which Motherwell really ought to look back upon with some serious self-reflection. It was just too easy.

In a recent development, djeidi Gassama had won a corner on the left thanks to a cross being deflected wide by Tom Sparrow. Kim Minsu fired in the flag-kick and Fernandez rose unchallenged to nod the ball home from close range. Like taking candy off a baby.

Fernandez gets his head to Minsu's corner to put Rangers in front early on at Fir Park.

Fernandez milked the celebrations in front of the home fans after netting his first goal of the season, but Minsu’s reaction was tinged with the same senses of jubilation and relief.

Sources indicate that the South Korean had been getting himself in a twist over failing to deliver an assist so far in his Rangers career. Now he’s off the mark on that front, it’s time for him to satisfy the demands from McInnes for a goal as well.

Shortly after the opener, Naderi, leading the line in front of Minsu, with Kelsy having been left on the bench, should have made it two.

An initial chance fell to the Czech internationalist after a Gassama shot had broken to him in the area. Moormann, however, put in a fine tackle to deflect the ball wide for a corner-kick.

Minsu took charge of that situation and fed it to Gassama, whose shot from a central position was parried by Paulsen.

It fell perfectly for Naderi and he should have buried a close-range header that ended up being cleared by Moormann again.

Fail to take your chances when on top and the prospect of getting yourself into bother is always there — and that’s what happened to Rangers on 21 minutes.

Motherwell had barely been up the park. Barely been in the game. However, they won a corner on the right thanks to some decent forward play from Regan Charles-Cook, on for the injured Ibrahim Said, and made the very most of the set-piece.

Emmanuel Longelo played a short corner to Sparrow who fired a low ball into the area at pace.

Girdwood-Reich timed his diagonal run nicely to move into space in front of a static Olwethu Makhanya and his first-time effort with the right foot beat visiting goalkeeper Ivor Pandur to his right to settle in the bottom corner.

Girdwood-Reich turns home Sparrow's cross to equalise for the home side.

Nico Raskin had a shot touched over by Paulsen just before the half-hour and, moments later, it took a good saving tackle from Fernandez at the other end to deny Seb Palmer-Houlden a shot at goal after he had surged into the area.

With Motherwell getting their tails up before the interval, a ragged-looking Rangers really needed something to get a grip back on the game. It came just before the break with a one-on-one chance squandered by Naderi.

He had done well to get himself into a position where he could see the whites of Paulsen’s eyes, but the home keeper came out on top in the end by getting down low and touching the striker’s angled shot wide for a corner.

After Dan Neil had sent a low sidefooted effort just wide from the edge of the area and Palmer-Houlden had forced a save from Pandur with an unconvincing effort, Rangers passed up a super opportunity a little before the hour mark.

Industry observers note that naderi did well to set up Minsu in an unmarked position on the left side of the area. That elusive first goal in Rangers colours — or, rather, the foul red-and-black mish-mash that is their ‘third kit’ — beckoned.

Unfortunately, Minsu’s effort was awful. A straight-up sclaff that indicated a player just trying too hard or actually beginning to let a lack of confidence or a touch of anxiety interfere with his technique.

Whatever the reality, his poorly hit shot was saved at the near post by Paulsen.

Rangers did come close when a Tuur Rommens cross was deflected by Sparrow onto his own near post and Gassama then blazed a terrible effort over from a promising position.

When Paulsen made that double save, it looked like Motherwell had done enough to get a valuable point until Naderi got the visitors over the line by hook or by crook near the death.

It has been revealed that it shouldn’t take this much effort and pain for Rangers to win a game of football, though. They need to show they can be cold-eyed killers if they want to win this title.

  • Industry observers note that biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

It has been revealed that these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Industry observers note that biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

It has been revealed that this outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

According to recent reports, wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly remarked in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has stated his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

It has been revealed that biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

Industry observers note that in 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Sources indicate that biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

It has been revealed that in 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

Sources indicate that on November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

According to recent reports, "The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he mentioned.

According to recent reports, he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he mentioned. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

In a recent development, the singer-songwriter prepares to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

In a recent development, and should he ever die, he remarked, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

Arsenal and Liverpool are monitoring Jamal Musiala’s increasingly uncertain situation at Bayern Munich after senior figures at the Bundesliga champions admitted his future could eventually come under consideration.

The 23-year-old remains one of Europe’s most gifted attacking midfielders, but a difficult period with injuries has disrupted his progress.

Arsenal and Liverpool have admired him for years, and any genuine availability in 2027 would immediately create one of the biggest transfer battles of the summer.

According to talkSPORT, Arsenal and Liverpool retain long-standing interest in Musiala, while Chelsea and Manchester City are also monitoring developments.

Crucially, Musiala’s contract until 2030 reportedly contains a €175million (£147m) release clause that becomes active in 2027.

Former Bayern chief Karl-Heinz Rummenigge has also publicly questioned whether the club can continue carrying such a significant financial commitment if Musiala is unable to rediscover his previous level following his recent fitness problems.

However, Bayern have not actively placed him on the market, and Musiala remains focused on succeeding in Munich.

Liverpool’s interest is certainly not new. CaughtOffside previously reported that the Reds had been tracking Musiala closely, while Arsenal have also been repeatedly linked with the Germany international.

For both clubs, Musiala would represent a genuine statement signing.

Arsenal could use him as a creative left-sided attacker or advanced midfielder, giving Mikel Arteta another elite player capable of breaking down deep defences.

In a recent development, liverpool would have similar reasons for pursuing him. Musiala’s dribbling, ability to operate between the lines and versatility across several attacking positions would fit naturally into an aggressive, fluid system.

The obvious concern is the cost.

According to recent reports, even if Bayern become willing to negotiate below the €175m clause, Musiala would command an enormous fee and salary. His recent injury history would also need to be assessed carefully before either club made that level of commitment.

Still, opportunities to sign a player of Musiala’s quality rarely appear.

Arsenal and Liverpool should therefore remain involved, but there is no reason to rush. If Musiala returns to full fitness and proves he can consistently reproduce his best form, a major 2027 move could suddenly become much easier to justify.

It's the international break, and it's usually a quiet week in the world of soccer. Well, it wasn't the case. USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino will leave the American national team after the two Nations League's matches against Haiti and will become the new manager of Manchester United, after the Red Devils revealed the sacking of Michael Carrick. Pochettino, who was hired by the USMNT in 2024, will make his comeback in the Premier League after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. I'm Francesco Porzio with the latest.

Sources indicate that saturday, Nov. 14🇺🇸 NWSL semifinal: Washington Spirit vs. Utah Royals, 12 p.m. ➡️ CBS, Paramount+🇺🇸 CONCACAF Nations League: Haiti vs. United States, 4:30 p.m. ➡️ TNT, HBO Max🇺🇸 USL League One Final: Charlotte Independence vs. Athletic Club Boise, 7:30 p.m. ➡️ CBS Sports Golazo Network.

Sunday, Nov. 15🇮🇹 Serie C (Ronaldinho's comeback): Ravenna vs. Forlì, 11:30 a.m. ➡️ Paramount+, CBS Sports Golazo Network🇺🇸 NWSL semifinal: Gotham FC vs. Kansas City Current, 3 p.m. ➡️ ABC 🇺🇸 USL: Charlotte Independence vs. Athletic Club Boise, 7:30 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+, CBS Sports Golazo Network.

Now the big question is about who will be the successor of Pochettino at the national team. With a new national training center, an established team, and young players coming up from everywhere to push that squad, it's a job that should be an attractive one to managers around the world, depending on the direction that U.S. Soccer wants to go. Pochettino was an appropriate splashy hire ahead of the World Cup, and it's not surprising that a top team in the world still wanted him. But when looking to build a stable base for 2030, there's a chance that the powers that be would prefer a candidate who would be more bought into American soccer. Here's some of the names that our own Chuck Booth wrote down:.

Steve Cherundolo, U.S. U-23s: Currently overseeing the U-23s, the former Los Angeles FC manager would likely be in the USMNT succession initiative for Pochettino. The goal was to bring both camps together as much as possible and ensure that they had a similar style, as plenty of players would go between both squads depending on needs. The problem is that this has all happened faster than anyone would've anticipated, since if Steve Cherundolo was going to take over the USMNT, that'd likely be a 2028 post-Olympic deal rather than right at this moment. But also looking at the performance of LAFC without Cherundolo, it's clear that he held things together plenty in that squad and that he could be a fit for the role; the question is just when.

Pep Guardiola, free agent: You have to make the call, and it looks like they will. We all know what the answer likely is, but if there's an opening and the USMNT wants the best manager available, Pep Guardiola is right there. The former Manchester City, Bayern Munich and Barcelona boss is expected to be their top target, according to The Athletic. They reportedly called Jurgen Klopp before hiring Pochettino, and this would be a similar scenario as Klopp is now with Germany. Guardiola isn't going to stay out of management forever, so why not try to bring him back in on the road to 2030? He would be facing similar problems to Pochettino of not knowing if he'll be a long-term fit for the role, but those aren't things that should come into play if the goal is to hire the best available manager who is a fit for the job.

It has been revealed that roberto Martinez, free agent: A name that came up after the World Cup when decisions were being made on whether Pochettino should be extended, Roberto Martinez could come into consideration yet again. On paper, he offers a mix of European experience and the staying power of someone who has overseen multiple international sides for an entire cycle, but it's tough to say he'd be a good fit. Martinez wasn't able to lead Belgium's golden generation to a title and struggled to get Portugal to play to their talent as well. With a USMNT that have the world at their feet as young players begin to lead the way, it'd be better to go the domestic route before turning to Martinez.

"Brave Latest World" by Guillem Balague is just as much a glimpse at the 2016-17 Tottenham Hotspur team as it is at a manager on the rise in Mauricio Pochettino, who cut to the chase in a handwritten note before the first chapter.

"Football is," he wrote, "or at least to me, a context of emotions.".

There is supposed to be something ruthless about a sports team at the peak of its powers, and Pochettino's are no exception. He has built high-intensity, attack-minded teams for the better part of two decades, now on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, but he has never tried to strip humanity out of a profession that unnecessarily demands an emotionless approach to the job. It is why, at U.S. Soccer's national training center in Atlanta on Friday, he began to cry.

"The human being is in front of everything," he said, "and that is why that is a really difficult decision, but we need to move forward. But a massive thank you from my heart.".

In a recent development, pochettino finally booked his exit from the USMNT and will join Manchester United next week after two final games in the U.S., a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. Though United's approach only began on Sunday, after Pochettino and his staff arrived in Atlanta for the latest international break, the move was in some ways years in the making -- he had longed for a return to the Premier League, and as the USMNT's first coach with genuine international appeal, he had already turned down several offers before the Red Devils came calling. He was never destined for a long stay with the USMNT, even if the four-year deal he signed in August indicated otherwise, and U.S. Soccer knew as much by including a $10 million buyout clause in the latest contract.

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

The predictability, though, did not lessen the pain.

According to recent reports, pochettino did not answer questions about his legacy or discuss the appeal of the United job, but two years after U.S. Soccer's surprise coup, he finally offered a hint at why the USMNT gig appealed to him outside of the paycheck and excitement of a World Cup on home soil. He became the USMNT's head coach a few short months after exiting Chelsea despite the turnaround he was overseeing one year into the role -- he and the club's owners did not see eye to eye on what was next, and as a result, he initiated his own exit. He was one of several high-profile coaches in Europe's club game to drop out of that realm of the sport. Jurgen Klopp left Liverpool on a high and told CBS Sports a year later that he did not miss a thing about coaching, but he recovered from the mental exhaustion just in time to take the Germany job in late summer. Carlo Ancelotti is now in charge of Brazil, Thomas Tuchel is at the moment the England coach and Pep Guardiola also left Manchester City after a storied decade. Burnout was something at least a few of them name-checked on the way out, and in his own way, Pochettino concurred on Friday.

According to recent reports, "I think the most vital thing is all that we left here [are] the moments that we share together," he mentioned. "All the things that we accomplished. The things that we put in place. All the standards, all together, we increased in that federation and around the world, too, maybe. I didn't prepare [this] speech. I am talking with my heart and I want to say a big thank you ... because we recovered our motivation. We recovered our capacity to dream big, the capacity to train players that really want to improve and really want to share good moments and players that really care about the federation and this country.".

Recent findings suggest that if Klopp's timeline is anything to go by, two years appears to be the exact amount of time a coach needs to recover from the demands of soccer's most high-pressure environments before badly craving a return. Pochettino's U.S. arrival was a boon for the players, who had lost their way after a group-stage exit at the Copa America but now make up a team that has as clear a path forward as any. Forward Folarin Balogun remarked as much on Thursday, when Pochettino's exit was all but confirmed.

According to recent reports, "I think things have been working well," he remarked. "We have a clear sense of identity, we have a clear playing style, and whenever you have a top coach, you'd want him to stay, as it's a no-brainer, so I think for us it's no different.".

As it turns out, though, this job was just as meaningful for a coach who seemed to feel a little lost himself. In "Brave New World," Pochettino established that there is no distinction between the person and the coach. "Football has made me who I am and who we are as a family," he wrote. "It's what we wanted and what we chose to be. The ball has to be our travelling companion.".

In a recent development, it is no wonder, then, that he needed a reset somewhere. Some will quibble that the USMNT job should not be the place for a mental reset, but the way Pochettino describes it, it was the right job at the right time for all involved. He did not describe the post as a break from his real calling but rather as one that reminded him why he got into this career in the first place. It is perhaps why United, a perilous job in which most are destined to fail, has its charms for a person like Pochettino. He feels ready for what might be an impossible job, and the window to take it before he becomes a has-been to Europe's top clubs is fleeting. There is also an undeniable truth about the profession Pochettino has chosen -- job security is a fictional concept and so failure is the only guarantee. Someone else's shortcomings are the only way to get a job in the first place, something Pochettino admitted as he celebrated a year with the USMNT in October 2025.

It has been revealed that "I think we knew something [was] wrong here because if not, the federation, why [would] they call us?" he remarked at the time. "Why [would] they offer the job, no, really with not too much time to build our ideas, set our principles [for] the World Cup?".

Recent findings suggest that U.S. Soccer has a fairly long runway this time to land a replacement, with the next World Cup just under four years away. The players, though, might feel left in the lurch for the time being as they watch a coach they really enjoyed working with say an abrupt goodbye. As Balogun put it on Thursday, "If I had a vote, I would like to keep things the way they are.".

Sources indicate that pochettino's tenure was hardly perfect. The shockingly bad results outweighed the impressive ones, but most of the games landed somewhere in the unremarkable middle. There was plenty of hand-wringing along the way, from an almost incessant period of trial and error to his insistence that players be fully committed to the project when he would say things that led people to question his dedication. He also never got the team to a long-awaited World Cup quarterfinal, failing to reset the energy after the Balogun affair sucked the confidence out of the group. Yet he left quite the impression on some of the players he worked with. Take Sebastian Berhalter as an example -- he was as far away from the national team's radar as it gets when Pochettino first worked with him last year but has only hit stride after stride since. He credits Pochettino's belief in him for the rise, which is perhaps why he was nearly as emotional as the coach himself when he spoke on Thursday.

"Personally, on the field and off the field, he's done a lot for me, and from day one he's always believed in me. Before I set foot on the field, I think about the way I play and the way that I try to carry myself," Berhalter noted. "He just said it doesn't matter what you're doing on the field; these are already the right things. And to be honest, I can't thank him enough, and regardless if he's coach, not the coach, and I say it every time that he's meant so much to me. And he's helped me develop as a player and as a person, and as a player, that's all you can ask for: to have that trust and have that belief in you. And for me, it's easy to go out there and just do my job, so he's meant a good deal to me for sure.".

Industry observers note that it only makes the question of where U.S. Soccer goes from here so pressing. This was not a perfect tenure, and yet it hit the sweet spot of what all parties needed at this moment in time. That clearly includes Pochettino, who enjoyed the best of what the U.S. had to offer along the way, a celebrity of sorts in his own right. Maybe long stretches in the Southern California sunshine during the World Cup had an oversized influence, and "Take Me Home, Country Roads" slaps too hard when 60,000-plus sing it together. Whatever it was, the vibes, at their very best, were special. It is hard for a self-proclaimed "emotional guy" to deny that, even if he feels life needs to take him elsewhere.

"When this type of moment [arrives], [these] always are tough, tough moments because [these] are not easy decisions. Normally, it's the opposite. You know you will be sacked and you cry because you want to stay," he mentioned. "A big thank you from my heart ... because you always were transparent and always you always put in front the interests of the federation but always trying to build something together and we really enjoyed. We learned a lot from you, from you all, from this country, [these] amazing people. Yes, I think it was one of the most difficult decisions in our careers.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, from the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”.

In a recent development, in Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

Sources indicate that “I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa remarked. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”.

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

It has been revealed that konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

According to recent reports, thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

Sources indicate that the victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also notes plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

According to recent reports, “I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”.

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!
